claim: In bilaterians and cnidarians, epithelial cell-polarity is regulated by the interactions between Par proteins, Wnt/PCP signaling pathway, and cell-cell adhesion.
source: In bilaterians and cnidarians, epithelial cell-polarity is regulated by the interactions between Par proteins, Wnt/PCP signaling pathway, and cell-cell adhesion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature throughout the manuscript and represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Par proteins are highly conserved across Metazoa, including ctenophores.
source: Par proteins are highly conserved across Metazoa, including ctenophores.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1-3 and citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: Ctenophore genomes lack components of the Wnt/PCP pathway and cell-cell adhesion complexes.
source: But strikingly, ctenophore genomes lack components of the Wnt/PCP pathway and cell-cell adhesion complexes raising the question if ctenophore cells are polarized by mechanisms involving Par proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies (Ryan et al., 2013) and comparative genomic analyses (Belahbib et al., 2018).

claim: MlPar-6 localizes to the apical cortex of cells during early M. leidyi development.
source: We show that these proteins distribute differently compared to what has been described for other animals, even though they segregate in a host-specific fashion when expressed in cnidarian embryos.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2 and quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements in Figure 2—figure supplements 8-10.

claim: MlPar-6 immunoreactivity is polarized to the animal cortex of the single cell zygote.
source: Although MlPar-6 immunoreactivity can be detected in the periphery of the entire cell, in all of over 100 specimens examined, its expression appears to be polarized to the animal cortex (determined by the position of the zygotic nucleus; Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplements 8–10) of the single cell zygote and to the apical (animal) cell cortex during every cleavage stage (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data from over 100 specimens shown in Figure 2A and quantitative analysis in Figure 2—figure supplements 8-10.

claim: MlPar-6 localizes to cell-contact-free regions facing the external media at the cortex during early cleavage stages.
source: At the cortex, MlPar-6 localizes to cell-contact-free regions facing the external media (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining images in Figure 2C showing MlPar-6 localization patterns.

claim: MlPar-6 becomes localized to the position of cell-cell contacts by 60 cell stage onwards.
source: Gradually through the next three hours of development, MlPar-6 becomes localized to the position of cell-cell contacts by 60 cell stage onwards (Figure 2—figure supplements 3E–G and 4).
evidence: This is shown through time-course immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplements 3E-G and 4.

claim: MlPar-6 is not localized in cells undergoing cellular movements during gastrulation.
source: During gastrulation (3–7 hpf; Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplements 3–4), MlPar-6 is not localized in cells undergoing cellular movements including the oral (four hpf; Figure 2—figure supplement 3G) and aboral ectoderm (5–6 hpf; Figure 2D) undergoing epibolic movements, syncytial endoderm, and mesenchymal 'mesoderm' (quotation marks its debatable homology).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data during gastrulation stages shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplements 3-4.

claim: MlPar-6 remains polarized in 'static' ectodermal cells at the animal pole and vegetal pole during gastrulation.
source: However, this protein remains polarized in 'static' ectodermal cells remaining at the animal pole (blastopore) and vegetal pole (4–7 hpf; Figure 2—figure supplements 3F–J and 4).
evidence: This is shown through immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplements 3F-J and 4.

claim: By the end of gastrulation (8-9 hpf), MlPar-6 becomes localized asymmetrically to the apical cortex of ectodermal epidermal cells and future ectodermal pharyngeal cells.
source: By the end of gastrulation (8–9 hpf; Figure 2E), MlPar-6 becomes localized asymmetrically to the apical cortex of the ectodermal epidermal cells and the future ectodermal pharyngeal cells that start folding inside the blastopore (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data at 8-9 hpf shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5A-C.

claim: MlPar-6 does not show clear cortical localization in later cydippid stages after 10 hpf.
source: Interestingly, we do not observe a clear cortical localization in later cydippid stages, and the antibody signal is weaker after 10 hpf in juveniles (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown through immunostaining data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: At later stages, MlPar-6 is cytosolic and does not localize in the cortex of epidermal cells.
source: Contrary to expectations, at these later stages, MlPar-6 is cytosolic and does not localize in the cortex of epidermal cells, and a few epithelial and mesenchymal cells showed nuclear localization (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 2F showing cytosolic and nuclear localization patterns.

claim: MlPar-6 remains cytosolic in all scored stages up to 24 hpf.
source: Thereafter, MlPar-6 remains cytosolic in all scored stages up to 24 hpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown through immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Cytosolic and nuclear localization of Par-6 has been reported in other organisms when the polarizing roles of this protein are inactive.
source: Cytosolic and nuclear localization of Par-6 has been reported in other organisms when the polarizing roles of this protein are inactive (Mizuno et al., 2003; Johansson et al., 2000; Cline and Nelson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in other organisms.

claim: MlPar-6 does not play a role in cell polarity during juvenile cydippid stages.
source: Thus, our data suggest that MlPar-6 does not play a role in cell polarity during juvenile cydippid stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the cytosolic localization pattern observed in later stages and comparison to known patterns in other organisms.

claim: MlPar-1 remains as punctate aggregations distributed uniformly in the cytosol during early M. leidyi development.
source: Even though MlPar-1 appears to be localized in the cortex at the cell-contact regions of early blastomeres and gastrula stages (Figure 3D–E), this antibody signal was not clear enough to be discriminated from the cytosolic distribution, possibly due to edge effects. Nevertheless, and strikingly, MlPar-1 remains as punctate aggregations distributed uniformly in the cytosol, and in some cases, co-distributes with chromosomes during mitosis (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MlPar-1 does not show asymmetric localization in the cell cortex of M. leidyi embryos at any observed stage.
source: We did not observe asymmetric localization of MlPar-1 in the cell cortex of M. leidyi embryos at any of the stages described above for MlPar-6.
evidence: This is based on comprehensive immunostaining analysis across all developmental stages examined.

claim: MlPar-6-mVenus localizes to the apical cell cortex during gastrulation and displays enrichment at the level of cell-cell contacts.
source: However, during gastrulation, MlPar-6-mVenus localizes to the apical cell cortex and displays enrichment at the level of cell-cell contacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging of MlPar-6-mVenus overexpression shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D-F.

claim: MlPar-6-mVenus cortical localization is no longer observable during cell movements associated with gastrulation.
source: As we observed by antibody staining, this cortical localization is no longer observable during the cell movements associated with gastrulation and MlPar-6-mVenus remains cytosolic (Figure 2—figure supplement 5D bottom).
evidence: This is shown through in vivo imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5D.

claim: After eight hpf, MlPar-6-mVenus localizes to the apical cortex of ectodermal epidermal and pharyngeal cells but is not observable in any other internal tissue.
source: After eight hpf, MlPar-6-mVenus localizes to the apical cortex of ectodermal epidermal and pharyngeal cells but is not observable in any other internal tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5G.

claim: After 10 hpf, MlPar-6-mVenus remains in the cytosol and no cortical localization was detectable.
source: After 10 hpf, MlPar-6-mVenus remains in the cytosol and no cortical localization was detectable (Figure 2—figure supplement 5H).
evidence: This is shown through in vivo imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5H.

claim: MlPar-1-mCherry localizes uniformly and forms aggregates in the cytosol during gastrulation.
source: Our in vivo observations on living embryos confirm the localization pattern described above by using MlPar-1 antibody at gastrula stages. MlPar-1-mCherry localizes uniformly and form aggregates in the cytosol during gastrulation (4–5 hpf; Figure 3—figure supplement 3D–E and Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging of MlPar-1-mCherry overexpression shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D-E and Video 1.

claim: MlPar-1-mCherry remains cytosolic in all cells at cydippid juvenile stages but is highly concentrated in the tentacle apparatus and underneath the endodermal canals.
source: This localization pattern remains throughout all recorded stages until cydippid juvenile stages where MlPar-1-mCherry remains cytosolic in all cells but is highly concentrated in the tentacle apparatus and underneath the endodermal canals (24 hpf; Figure 3—figure supplement 3F–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and Video 2).
evidence: This is shown through in vivo imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, and Video 2.

claim: In N. vectensis embryos, MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry symmetrically distribute during early cleavage stages.
source: In N. vectensis embryos, MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry symmetrically distribute during early cleavage stages (Figure 4A and C) and both proteins localize asymmetrically only after blastula formation (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo imaging of ctenophore proteins expressed in cnidarian embryos shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Both MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry translated proteins display the same pattern as the previously described endogenous N. vectensis Par-6 and Par-1 proteins when expressed in N. vectensis.
source: In these experiments, both MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry translated proteins display the same pattern as the previously described endogenous N. vectensis Par-6 and Par-1 proteins (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the localization patterns in Figure 4 with previously published data on N. vectensis Par proteins.

claim: The protein structure of ctenophore MlPar-6 and MlPar-1 contains the necessary information to localize as other bilaterians proteins do.
source: These data suggest that the protein structure of ctenophore MlPar-6 and MlPar-1 contains the necessary information to localize as other bilaterians proteins do.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterologous expression experiments showing proper localization in cnidarian hosts.

claim: In bilaterians and cnidarians, a polarized epithelium is classically defined as a group of polarized cells joined by belt-like cell-cell junctions and supported by a basement membrane.
source: In bilaterians and cnidarians, a polarized epithelium is classically defined as a group of polarized cells joined by belt-like cell-cell junctions and supported by a basement membrane (Magie and Martindale, 2008; St Johnston and Sanson, 2011; Thompson, 2013; Ohno et al., 2015; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature defining epithelial tissue organization.

claim: The asymmetric cortical distribution of the Wnt Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) pathway components polarizes the cells along the tissue plane.
source: While the asymmetric cortical distribution of the Wnt Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) pathway components polarizes the cells along the tissue plane, the asymmetric cortical distribution of Par system components polarizes the cells along the apical-basal axis (St Johnston and Sanson, 2011; Thompson, 2013; Gumbiner and Kim, 2014; Besson et al., 2015; Yang and Mlodzik, 2015; Ahmed and Macara, 2016; Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016; Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Davey and Moens, 2017; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Fanto and McNeill, 2004; St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010; Cha et al., 2011; Kumburegama et al., 2011; Nance and Zallen, 2011; Momose et al., 2012; Wallingford, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to literature on cell polarity mechanisms.

claim: The asymmetric cortical distribution of Par system components polarizes the cells along the apical-basal axis.
source: While the asymmetric cortical distribution of the Wnt Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) pathway components polarizes the cells along the tissue plane, the asymmetric cortical distribution of Par system components polarizes the cells along the apical-basal axis (St Johnston and Sanson, 2011; Thompson, 2013; Gumbiner and Kim, 2014; Besson et al., 2015; Yang and Mlodzik, 2015; Ahmed and Macara, 2016; Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016; Butler and Wallingford, 2017; Davey and Moens, 2017; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Fanto and McNeill, 2004; St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010; Cha et al., 2011; Kumburegama et al., 2011; Nance and Zallen, 2011; Momose et al., 2012; Wallingford, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to literature on cell polarity mechanisms.

claim: The mechanisms that organize cell-polarity are highly conserved in all animals that have been studied and most likely been present in the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of Cnidaria and Bilateria.
source: The mechanisms that organize cell-polarity are highly conserved in all animals that have been studied and most likely been present in the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of Cnidaria and Bilateria (Thompson, 2013; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Kumburegama et al., 2011; Momose et al., 2012; Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Ragkousi et al., 2017; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2018; Belahbib et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Ctenophores possess a stereotyped development.
source: Interestingly, ctenophores or comb jellies, whose position at the base of metazoan tree is still under debate (Dunn et al., 2008; Hejnol et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2013; Moroz et al., 2014; Whelan et al., 2017), (Simion et al., 2017), (Feuda et al., 2017), possess a stereotyped development (Figure 1B) and do not have the genes that encode the components of the Wnt/PCP pathway in their genomes (Ryan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is shown through the developmental diagram in Figure 1B and supported by citations.

claim: Ctenophores do not have the genes that encode the components of the Wnt/PCP pathway in their genomes.
source: Interestingly, ctenophores or comb jellies, whose position at the base of metazoan tree is still under debate (Dunn et al., 2008; Hejnol et al., 2009; Ryan et al., 2013; Moroz et al., 2014; Whelan et al., 2017), (Simion et al., 2017), (Feuda et al., 2017), possess a stereotyped development (Figure 1B) and do not have the genes that encode the components of the Wnt/PCP pathway in their genomes (Ryan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic study (Ryan et al., 2013).

claim: The asymmetric localization of the Crumbs (Crb) complex, the Par/aPKC complex, and the Scribble complex in the cortex of bilaterian and cnidarian cells maintains epithelial integrity by stabilizing cell-cell junctions.
source: The asymmetric localization of the Crumbs (Crb) complex, (e.g. Crb/Pals1/Patj), the Par/aPKC complex (e.g. Par-3/aPKC/Par-6), and the Scribble complex (e.g. Scribble/Lgl/Dlg) in the cortex of bilaterian and cnidarian cells maintains epithelial integrity by stabilizing cell-cell junctions (Ohno et al., 2015; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2018; Belahbib et al., 2018) via the Cadherin-Catenin complex (CCC) of mature Adherens Junctions (AJs) (Magie and Martindale, 2008; Belahbib et al., 2018; Harris and Peifer, 2004; Nelson and Nusse, 2004; McGill et al., 2009; Oda and Takeichi, 2011; Schäfer et al., 2014; Weng and Wieschaus, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to literature on cell polarity complexes and junctional stability.

claim: The maturation of AJs is essential for the maintenance of the Par/aPKC complex localization at the apical cortex that displaces members of the Scribble complex and Par-1 to basolateral localizations associated with Septate Junctions (SJs).
source: The maturation of AJs is essential for the maintenance of the Par/aPKC complex localization at the apical cortex that displaces members of the Scribble complex and Par-1 to basolateral localizations associated with Septate Junctions (SJs) (Belahbib et al., 2018; Benton and St Johnston, 2003; Hurov et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2007; Iden and Collard, 2008; Yamanaka and Ohno, 2008; Oshima and Fehon, 2011; Ganot et al., 2015; Humbert et al., 2015; Kharfallah et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on adherens junction maturation and polarity complex localization.

claim: This mechanism is deployed in bilaterian cells to establish embryonic and epithelial cell polarity during early development and is critical for axial organization.
source: This mechanism is deployed in bilaterian cells to establish embryonic and epithelial cell polarity during early development and is critical for axial organization (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Cha et al., 2011; Munro, 2006; Patalano et al., 2006; Goldstein and Macara, 2007; Weisblat, 2007; Alford et al., 2009; Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Doerflinger et al., 2010; Chan and Nance, 2013; Lang and Munro, 2017; Tepass, 2012; Nance and Zallen, 2011; Weng and Wieschaus, 2017; Zhu et al., 2017; Ragkousi et al., 2017; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2018; Schneider and Bowerman, 2003; Macara, 2004; Vinot et al., 2004; Dollar et al., 2005; Ossipova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to literature on early development and axial patterning.

claim: Components of the Par system are unique to, and highly conserved, across Metazoa, including placozoans, poriferans, and ctenophores.
source: Components of the Par system are unique to, and highly conserved, across Metazoa, including placozoans, poriferans, and ctenophores (Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: Ctenophore genomes do not have many of the crucial regulators present in other metazoan genomes.
source: But strikingly, ctenophore genomes do not have many of the crucial regulators present in other metazoan genomes (Belahbib et al., 2018; Ganot et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: None of the components of the Crb complex, a Scribble homolog, or Human and Drosophila SJs, are present in ctenophore genomes.
source: For example, none of the components of the Crb complex, a Scribble homolog, or Human and Drosophila SJs, are present (Belahbib et al., 2018; Ganot et al., 2015), and the cytoplasmic domain of cadherin lacks the crucial biding sites to catenins that interact with the actin cytoskeleton (Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of ctenophore cadherin lacks the crucial binding sites to catenins that interact with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: For example, none of the components of the Crb complex, a Scribble homolog, or Human and Drosophila SJs, are present (Belahbib et al., 2018; Ganot et al., 2015), and the cytoplasmic domain of cadherin lacks the crucial biding sites to catenins that interact with the actin cytoskeleton (Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic study.

claim: The MlPar-6 antibody is specific to M. leidyi Par-6 protein.
source: Pre-adsorption of the antibodies with a tenfold excess of the antigen peptide resulted in the elimination of the staining of the appropriate-sized single band for MlPar-6 and MlPar-1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and peptide competition assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MlPar-1 antibody is specific to M. leidyi Par-1 protein.
source: Pre-adsorption of the antibodies with a tenfold excess of the antigen peptide resulted in the elimination of the staining of the appropriate-sized single band for MlPar-6 and MlPar-1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot and peptide competition assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is only a single copy for both Par-6 (MlPar-6) and Par-1 (MlPar-1) genes in the M. leidyi genome.
source: Genome searches of M. leidyi showed that there is only a single copy for both Par-6 (MlPar-6) and Par-1 (MlPar-1) genes and they express through development in the transcriptome of M. leidyi (Babonis, 2018; Levin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome and transcriptome studies.

claim: MlPar-6 and MlPar-1 genes express through development in the transcriptome of M. leidyi.
source: Genome searches of M. leidyi showed that there is only a single copy for both Par-6 (MlPar-6) and Par-1 (MlPar-1) genes and they express through development in the transcriptome of M. leidyi (Babonis, 2018; Levin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptome studies.

claim: The components of the ctenophore MlPar/aPKC complex (MlPar-3/MlaPKC/MlPar-6 and MlCdc42) are highly conserved and contain all the domains present in other metazoans.
source: The components of the ctenophore MlPar/aPKC complex (MlPar-3/MlaPKC/MlPar-6 and MlCdc42) are highly conserved and contain all the domains present in other metazoans (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2; Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2 and supported by citations.

claim: The primary structure of MlPar-1 protein is highly conserved and contains all the domains (with the same amino acid length) required for its proper functioning in other metazoans.
source: Similarly, the primary structure of MlPar-1 protein (a Serine/threonine-protein kinase) is highly conserved and contains all the domains (with the same amino acid length) required for its proper functioning in other metazoans (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Belahbib et al., 2018), and localizes to the lateral cortex when expressed in cnidarian embryos (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and supported by citations.

claim: MlPar-1 localizes to the lateral cortex when expressed in cnidarian embryos.
source: Similarly, the primary structure of MlPar-1 protein (a Serine/threonine-protein kinase) is highly conserved and contains all the domains (with the same amino acid length) required for its proper functioning in other metazoans (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Belahbib et al., 2018), and localizes to the lateral cortex when expressed in cnidarian embryos (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by heterologous expression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ctenophores do not have homologs for any of the Crb complex components.
source: Recent studies have shown that ctenophores do not have homologs for any of the Crb complex components (Belahbib et al., 2018), required for the proper stabilization of the CCC and Par/aPKC complex in other studied taxa (Ohno et al., 2015; Harris and Peifer, 2004; Tepass, 2012; Chalmers et al., 2005; Hayase et al., 2013; Whitney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic study.

claim: The lack of MlPar-6 polarization during later stages is congruent with the absence of Crb complex components.
source: The lack of MlPar-6 (Figure 2) polarization during later stages is totally congruent with these observations, indicating that Par proteins in ctenophores do not have the necessary interactions to stabilize apico-basal cell polarity in their cells as in other animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of localization data and genomic information.

claim: Par proteins in ctenophores do not have the necessary interactions to stabilize apico-basal cell polarity in their cells as in other animals.
source: The lack of MlPar-6 (Figure 2) polarization during later stages is totally congruent with these observations, indicating that Par proteins in ctenophores do not have the necessary interactions to stabilize apico-basal cell polarity in their cells as in other animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of localization data and genomic information about missing components.

claim: Ctenophore species do not have the molecular components to form SJs and lack a Scribble homolog.
source: In addition, ctenophore species do not have the molecular components to form SJs and lack a Scribble homolog (Belahbib et al., 2018; Ganot et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: The lack of SJ components and Scribble homolog could explain the cytosolic localization of MlPar-1 during the observed stages.
source: This could explain the cytosolic localization of MlPar-1 during the observed stages (Benton and St Johnston, 2003; Iden and Collard, 2008; Humbert et al., 2015; Bilder et al., 2000; Vaccari et al., 2005), (Bonello et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of localization data and genomic information, supported by citations to literature on Par-1 localization mechanisms.

claim: Ctenophore species lack the full set of cell-cell adhesion proteins as known in other metazoans, including Placozoans and Poriferans.
source: Furthermore, ctenophore species do not have the full set of cell-cell adhesion proteins (Belahbib et al., 2018; Ryan et al., 2013; Ganot et al., 2015) as we know them in other metazoans, including Placozoans and Poriferans (Magie and Martindale, 2008; Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: The cadherin of ctenophores does not have the cytoplasmic domains required to bind any of the catenins of the CCC.
source: The cadherin of ctenophores does not have the cytoplasmic domains required to bind any of the catenins of the CCC (e.g. p120, alpha- and ß-catenin) (Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic study.

claim: Neither the actin nor microtubule cytoskeleton can be linked to ctenophore cadherin through the CCC.
source: This implies that neither the actin nor microtubule cytoskeleton can be linked to ctenophore cadherin through the CCC, as seen essential in other metazoans to stabilize pre-existent Par proteins polarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of catenin-binding domains in ctenophore cadherin.

claim: There are additional mechanisms that integrate the cytoskeleton of ctenophore cells with their cell-cell adhesion system.
source: This suggests that there are additional mechanisms that integrate the cytoskeleton of ctenophore cells with their cell-cell adhesion system.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that ctenophores have epithelia despite lacking classical adhesion machinery.

claim: The conservation of an organized 'Par-dependent epithelium' cannot be extended to all Eumetazoa.
source: In conclusion, regardless the phylogenetic position of the Ctenophora, the conservation of an organized 'Par-dependent epithelium' cannot be extended to all Eumetazoa.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing different Par protein localization patterns in ctenophores compared to other metazoans.

claim: Ctenophore cells do not have other essential components to organize the polarizing function of the Par system as in other studied metazoans.
source: Ctenophore cells do not have other essential components to organize the polarizing function of the Par system as in other studied metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data showing absence of key polarity regulators.

claim: Ctenophore cells do not deploy and/or stabilize the asymmetrical localization of Par-6 and Par-1 proteins.
source: Despite the high structural conservation of Par proteins across Metazoa, we have shown that ctenophore cells do not deploy and/or stabilize the asymmetrical localization of Par-6 and Par-1 proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the immunostaining and live imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ctenophore tissues organize their epithelium in a different way than the classical definition seen in bilaterians.
source: Thus, ctenophore tissues organize their epithelium in a different way than the classical definition seen in bilaterians.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of localization data and genomic information.

claim: The absence of Par protein localization and Wnt/PCP pathways in ctenophores implies that a new set of interactions emerged at least in the Cnidaria+Bilateria ancestor.
source: Unless the lack of Par protein localization in M. leidyi is a secondary loss, the absence of these pathways in ctenophores implies that a new set of interactions emerged at least in the Cnidaria+Bilateria ancestor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and that, could have regulated the way by which the Par system polarizes embryonic and epithelial cells.
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on the comparative data and phylogenetic considerations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In bilaterians, the asymmetric localization of Par/aPKC complex is established and maintained since the earliest stages of development.
source: While in the studied bilaterians this asymmetry is established and maintained since the earliest stages of development (Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Lang and Munro, 2017; Zhu et al., 2017; Nance, 2014; Hoege and Hyman, 2013; Von Stetina and Mango, 2015), in the cnidarian N. vectensis there is no early asymmetrical localization of any of the Par components (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Ragkousi et al., 2017) and embryonic polarity is controlled by the Wnt signaling system (Kumburegama et al., 2011; Wikramanayake et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2007; Martindale and Hejnol, 2009; Martindale and Lee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on bilaterian development.

claim: In the cnidarian N. vectensis there is no early asymmetrical localization of any of the Par components.
source: While in the studied bilaterians this asymmetry is established and maintained since the earliest stages of development (Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Lang and Munro, 2017; Zhu et al., 2017; Nance, 2014; Hoege and Hyman, 2013; Von Stetina and Mango, 2015), in the cnidarian N. vectensis there is no early asymmetrical localization of any of the Par components (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Ragkousi et al., 2017) and embryonic polarity is controlled by the Wnt signaling system (Kumburegama et al., 2011; Wikramanayake et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2007; Martindale and Hejnol, 2009; Martindale and Lee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on N. vectensis.

claim: In N. vectensis, embryonic polarity is controlled by the Wnt signaling system.
source: While in the studied bilaterians this asymmetry is established and maintained since the earliest stages of development (Munro and Bowerman, 2009; Lang and Munro, 2017; Zhu et al., 2017; Nance, 2014; Hoege and Hyman, 2013; Von Stetina and Mango, 2015), in the cnidarian N. vectensis there is no early asymmetrical localization of any of the Par components (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Ragkousi et al., 2017) and embryonic polarity is controlled by the Wnt signaling system (Kumburegama et al., 2011; Wikramanayake et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2007; Martindale and Hejnol, 2009; Martindale and Lee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Wnt signaling in cnidarians.

claim: Once epithelial tissues form and epithelial cell-polarity is established in both bilaterian and cnidarian species, the asymmetric localization of Par proteins become highly polarized and is maintained through development.
source: In spite of these differences, once epithelial tissues form and epithelial cell-polarity is established in both bilaterian and cnidarian species, the asymmetric localization of Par proteins become highly polarized and is maintained through development.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Par-mediated apicobasal cell polarity is responsible for the maturation and maintenance of cell-cell adhesion in epithelial tissue.
source: In those cases, Par-mediated apicobasal cell polarity is responsible for the maturation and maintenance of cell-cell adhesion in epithelial tissue (Ohno et al., 2015; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Par protein function.

claim: The polarizing activity of the Par system was already present in epithelial cells of the MRCA between Bilateria and Cnidaria.
source: We have suggested that the polarizing activity of the Par system was already present in epithelial cells of the MRCA between Bilateria and Cnidaria (Salinas-Saavedra and Martindale, 2018; Salinas-Saavedra and Martindale, 2018) and could be extended to all Metazoa, where these proteins are present (including ctenophores, sponges, and placozoans Fahey and Degnan, 2010; Belahbib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an evolutionary inference based on comparative data and supported by citations.

claim: In bilaterians, the apical localization of Par-6 induces the phosphorylation of Par-1, displacing this protein to basolateral cortical regions.
source: In bilaterians and cnidarians, the apical localization of MlPar-6 induces the phosphorylation of MlPar-1, displacing this protein to basolateral cortical regions (Ohno et al., 2015; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Ragkousi et al., 2017; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Par protein interactions.

claim: The punctuate aggregates of MlPar-1-mCherry are highly dynamic and move throughout the entire cytosol.
source: Interestingly, the punctuate aggregates of MlPar-1-mCherry are highly dynamic and move throughout the entire cytosol (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting a potential association with cytoskeletal components (see Video 1) as MlPar-1 conserve these motifs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Video 1.

claim: MlPar-1 may be associated with cytoskeletal components.
source: Interestingly, the punctuate aggregates of MlPar-1-mCherry are highly dynamic and move throughout the entire cytosol (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting a potential association with cytoskeletal components (see Video 1) as MlPar-1 conserve these motifs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the dynamic movement patterns observed and conservation of cytoskeletal-binding motifs.

claim: In bilaterians, the Wnt/PCP signaling pathway antagonizes the action of the Par/aPKC complex.
source: For example, in bilaterians the Wnt/PCP signaling pathway antagonizes the action of the Par/aPKC complex (Cha et al., 2011; Besson et al., 2015; Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016; Humbert et al., 2015; Humbert et al., 2006; Seifert and Mlodzik, 2007), so this may explain the lack of polarization in ctenophore tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on Wnt/PCP and Par interactions.

claim: The lack of Wnt/PCP pathway in ctenophores may explain the lack of polarization in ctenophore tissue.
source: For example, in bilaterians the Wnt/PCP signaling pathway antagonizes the action of the Par/aPKC complex (Cha et al., 2011; Besson et al., 2015; Aigouy and Le Bivic, 2016; Humbert et al., 2015; Humbert et al., 2006; Seifert and Mlodzik, 2007), so this may explain the lack of polarization in ctenophore tissue.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known antagonistic relationship between Wnt/PCP and Par systems in other organisms.

claim: Different mechanisms might have co-opted to generate similar epithelial morphologies in different metazoan lineages.
source: Under this definition, a 'Par-dependent epithelium' may have a single origin in Metazoa, but, different mechanisms might have co-opted to generate similar epithelial morphologies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an evolutionary hypothesis based on the comparative data presented and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ctenophore epithelia, N. vectensis endomesoderm, and Drosophila midgut represent cases where epithelial cells are highly polarized along the apical-basal axis but this polarization does not depend on Par proteins.
source: Ctenophore epithelia, along with other recent works in N. vectensis endomesoderm (Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2015; Salinas-Saavedra et al., 2018) and Drosophila midgut (Chen et al., 2018), suggest this possibility. In all these cases, epithelial cells are highly polarized along the apical-basal axis, but this polarization does not depend on Par proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in this study and citations to other studies showing Par-independent epithelial polarity.

claim: MlPar-6 displays statistically significant apical enrichment compared to basal regions during early developmental stages (1-cell through 9 hpf).
source: Different MlPar-6 localization between basal and apical cortex for each stage represented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 8. Median, 95% CI, and P values are depicted in the figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 10.

claim: MlPar-6 does not show statistically significant apical enrichment at 10 hpf and 11 hpf stages.
source: Different MlPar-6 localization between basal and apical cortex for each stage represented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 8. Median, 95% CI, and P values are depicted in the figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements showing P values of 0.4070 (ns) and 0.3217 (ns) for 10 hpf and 11 hpf respectively in Figure 2—figure supplement 10.

claim: MlPar-1 does not show statistically significant differences between basal and apical localization at 4-cell, 8-cell, 5-6 hpf, and 8-9 hpf stages.
source: Fluorescent intensity (Y axis) was measured along the basal/apical axes (X axis) for the developmental stages reported in Figure 3. Numerical data can be found in Figure 3—figure supplement 5—source data 1 and 2. Median, 95% CI, and P values are depicted in the figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: MlPar-6-mVenus shows no statistically significant asymmetric localization during early cleavage stages in N. vectensis embryos.
source: Fluorescent intensity (Y axis) was measured along the basal/apical axes (X axis) for the developmental stages reported in Figure 4. All measured cells display asymmetric localization of MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry during later stages. Median, 95% CI, and P values are depicted in the figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative measurements showing P value = 0.5775 (ns) for Par-6 Early stage in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MlPar-6-mVenus shows statistically significant apical localization during late gastrula stages in N. vectensis embryos.
source: Fluorescent intensity (Y axis) was measured along the basal/apical axes (X axis) for the developmental stages reported in Figure 4. All measured cells display asymmetric localization of MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry during later stages. Median, 95% CI, and P values are depicted in the figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative measurements showing P value = 2.470e-016 for Par-6 Late stage in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MlPar-1-mCherry shows statistically significant basolateral localization during late gastrula stages in N. vectensis embryos.
source: Fluorescent intensity (Y axis) was measured along the basal/apical axes (X axis) for the developmental stages reported in Figure 4. All measured cells display asymmetric localization of MlPar-6-mVenus and MlPar-1-mCherry during later stages. Median, 95% CI, and P values are depicted in the figure.
